sections.title: Mission · Work with Temporary Data and Links
paragraphs: The final Linux Essentials objective focuses on temporary directories, special permissions, and symbolic links.
sections.callout: TEMPORARY DATA · SHARED-DIRECTORY PROTECTION · PATHNAME POINTERS

sections.title: Temporary Files
paragraphs: Applications and users create temporary files for short-term working data. Linux provides standard shared locations with different persistence expectations.

sections.title: /tmp/
paragraphs: /tmp/ is used for temporary working data and is generally treated as more transient; cleanup policies can remove its contents.

sections.title: /var/tmp/
paragraphs: /var/tmp/ is also temporary storage but is intended for data that should persist longer, often across reboots depending on system policy.

table.caption: Temporary data lifetime
rows: Temporary but intended to persist longer

sections.title: Shared Temporary Directories Create a Problem
paragraphs: A shared writable directory must let many users create files without letting every user delete or rename everyone else's files. Ordinary write access alone does not solve this safely.

sections.title: Sticky Bit
paragraphs: The sticky bit on a shared writable directory restricts deletion or renaming so users cannot inappropriately remove one another's files.

sections.title: Recognizing the Sticky Bit
paragraphs: In a long permission listing, a final t in the others execute position indicates the sticky bit, as commonly seen on /tmp/.

sections.title: Exam Trap · Sticky Bit
paragraphs: The sticky bit does not make a directory read-only. It protects files in a shared writable directory against unauthorized deletion or renaming.

sections.title: Symbolic Links
paragraphs: A symbolic link, or symlink, is a pathname pointer to another file or directory.
sections.callout: SYMBOLIC LINK = POINTER TO ANOTHER PATH

sections.title: Why Symbolic Links Are Useful
paragraphs: Symbolic links provide alternate paths, convenient names, and flexible references without duplicating the target's data.

sections.title: ln -s
paragraphs: ln -s creates a symbolic link. The pattern is ln -s TARGET LINK: first the existing target, then the new pointer name.

sections.title: Exam Trap · Source and Link Order
paragraphs: Remember: what exists first, then what pointer should be created. ln -s TARGET LINK.

sections.title: Symbolic Link Behavior
paragraphs: A symlink references its target path. If the target is removed or moved, the link can remain but become broken.
sections.callout: LINK EXISTS + TARGET GONE = BROKEN SYMLINK

table.caption: Duplicate versus pointer
rows: Pointer or reference to a target

sections.title: ls -d
paragraphs: ls -d lists the directory entry itself rather than listing the directory's contents. The d option here does not mean delete.
sections.callout: ls -d = SHOW THE DIRECTORY ENTRY ITSELF
